research_question: Can a best-possible-world argument for the existence of God rely on mathematical elegance as a source of intrinsic value if that value does not require a conscious valuer?

argument.title: Best‑Possible‑World Theodicy
argument.paper_title: A Theological Argument for an Everett Multiverse

premises.text: The actual world is the best possible world.
premises.quote: The actual world is the best possible world.

premises.text: Total goodness of the world is the intrinsic value—pleasure minus suffering—of all conscious experiences.
premises.quote: But when I consider the total goodness of the world, I do mean intrinsic value—pleasure minus suffering, happiness minus unhappiness, joy minus agony—of all conscious experiences that occur.

premises.text: Our universe contains both happiness and suffering, so its intrinsic happiness alone is unlikely to be maximal.
premises.quote: Now I have personally experienced a lot of happiness in my life, and I have seen many other people appear to be happy, so I do think that our universe does have considerable positive intrinsic value. But there is also much suffering and unhappiness, so it does not seem very plausible that the intrinsic happiness within this universe alone is the maximum logically possible.

premises.text: The universe’s high mathematical elegance adds to its intrinsic value.
premises.quote: However, besides the mixed happiness that our universe contains, our universe seems to have a very high degree of mathematical elegance and beauty. Humans can partially appreciate some of this elegance, so it does seem to increase the intrinsic value of the universe.

premises.text: A Being outside the universe could have enormous appreciation for its mathematical elegance.
premises.quote: But if one considers the possibility that there may be a Being outside the universe that has an enormous appreciation for the mathematical elegance of the universe, and perhaps an even greater appreciation if that Being were the Creator of the universe, then it seems that the hypothesis that the actual world is the best possible world might plausibly lead to what I call the Optimal Argument for the Existence of God as such a Being outside the universe who created and experiences tremendous value in having much greater knowledge and appreciation for the mathematical elegance of the universe than we creatures within the universe can have.

premises.text: The best‑possible‑world hypothesis fits better with a world containing an omniscient, omnipotent, omnibenevolent God than with a world where the universe stands alone.
premises.quote: The hypothesis that the actual world is the best possible world certainly appears to me to be more consistent with a world with an omniscient, omnipotent, omnibenevolent Being (which I shall henceforth call God, since these are the main properties traditionally assigned to God), than with a world in which our universe stands alone, with its mathematical elegance not fully appreciated.

missing_premise.text: If the actual world is the best possible world, then an omniscient, omnipotent, omnibenevolent God exists who creates and values a mathematically elegant universe.

conclusion.text: From the best‑possible‑world hypothesis it follows that an omniscient, omnipotent, omnibenevolent God exists who creates and values a mathematically elegant universe.

argument.skeleton: A; B; C -> E; F; G; H |- D

challenged_premise.text: Mathematical elegance adds to a world's intrinsic value only when it is appreciated by a suitable Being, so that its added value is relational to that appreciation rather than wholly independent of any valuer.

objection: Consider a sealed universe, call it Lattice, containing only a vast, perfectly symmetric crystalline structure governed by one compact law. No conscious being ever exists in Lattice, and no mind, finite or infinite, is positioned to appreciate it. Its symmetries still hold, and they still make the world more intricate, more economical, and more unified than a comparable disordered world with the same quantity of matter. Remove every valuer and the structure remains exactly as elegant, so its elegance cannot be relational to any appreciation. The premise's 'only when' clause therefore fails: elegance can add intrinsic value with no suitable Being present. If elegance adds value in Lattice independently of any valuer, the premise cannot secure the claim that a God must exist to appreciate it, because the appreciation it requires is not necessary for the value it is supposed to supply.

strongest_responses.response: Restricted the 'only when' clause to the value elegance contributes to worlds containing conscious experiences, conceding that Lattice may contain non-relational elegance-value but denying that this affects the actual world's case.
strongest_responses.why_it_failed: Defender A conceded that the argument does not survive as stated because the inference from elegance-value to God's necessary appreciation collapses if elegance can have value without a valuer, and the restriction to experiential worlds appears ad hoc.

strongest_responses.response: Recast unappreciated elegance as axiologically inert, analogous to unfelt pleasure, and proposed that while unappreciated elegance might retain minor independent value, only the conscious appreciation of a suitable Being provides sufficient value to offset suffering and make a world the best possible.
strongest_responses.why_it_failed: The objector's intuition that Lattice gains value from its symmetries directly contests the analogy to unfelt pleasure, and Defender B conceded that the original 'only when' clause was stronger than needed, retreating to a weaker claim that unappreciated value is insufficient for the argument's conclusion.

open_questions: Is the analogy between unappreciated mathematical elegance and unfelt pleasure metaphysically sound, or does structural elegance possess axiological properties that unconscious states lack?

If mathematical elegance can add intrinsic value without a valuer in non-experiential worlds like Lattice, what principled reason restricts its value-adding role to appreciation in worlds that happen to contain consciousness?

How much non-relational elegance-value is required to undermine the inference that an omniscient appreciator is necessary for the best possible world, and can a theist consistently concede minor unappreciated value while maintaining that divine appreciation is essential?
paper_direction: A paper here would argue that theistic arguments from the best possible world face a dilemma when they invoke mathematical elegance as a source of intrinsic value: if elegance adds value non-relationally, as the Lattice case suggests, then a divine appreciator is not necessary for that value; if elegance adds value only through appreciation, then the argument must defend a restriction to experiential worlds that appears ad hoc. The case would develop the Lattice thought experiment to show that unappreciated structural properties such as symmetry, economy, and unity generate genuine intrinsic value independent of any valuer. The strongest reply to anticipate is the theistic retreat to a weaker premise that analogizes unappreciated elegance to unfelt pleasure and claims that only the conscious appreciation of a suitable Being supplies value sufficient to offset suffering and make a world best. The paper would need to show that this restricted premise either begs the question against non-relational axiologies or is metaphysically unmotivated, and that conceding even minor non-relational elegance-value is enough to break the inference from elegance to the necessary existence of God.

reasons.coherence: The objection's key inference from 'still elegant' to 'value not relational' is a non sequitur, and its dilemma misdescribes the relational horn as needing an ad hoc restriction when it simply follows the argument's own experientialist premise c008.
reasons.robustness: Neither the case nor the plan answers the obvious replies that Lattice merely restates a contested Moorean intuition and that appreciated elegance can add value on top of any non-relational value; the plan assumes the theist's weaker premise is question-begging rather than showing it.
reasons.significance: Even if it succeeded, it would mostly replay the old Moore–Sidgwick dispute in a new setting and would at most remove one supporting consideration in a single idiosyncratic argument, leaving the creator-based inference intact.
reasons.specificity: There is a definite dilemma thesis and a named case, but the plan for showing the restricted premise 'begs the question or is unmotivated' is undeveloped and the relevant literature is not identified.

assessment.strongest_objection: The Lattice case conflates elegance with elegance-value: 'remove every valuer and the structure remains exactly as elegant' is fully compatible with the premise, which makes only the value relational, not the elegance. The claim that Lattice is nonetheless better is just Moore's unobserved-beautiful-world intuition, which the argument's own c008 (total goodness is the value of conscious experiences) already rejects, so the objection begs the question against the argument's stated axiology. And even if some non-relational elegance-value is granted, the theist can hold that divinely appreciated elegance adds further value, and the conditional premise also grounds God as creator, not only as appreciator, so the inference to God does not collapse.
assessment.what_it_needs: It must separate elegance from its value, engage the Moore–Sidgwick debate on unobserved beauty and Page's actual argument, and confront c008 directly rather than through a bare counterexample. It must also show that conceding non-relational elegance-value defeats the additive 'appreciation adds more' reply and the creator role of God, not merely the appreciator role.
assessment.summary: As framed this would be dismissed quickly, because it confuses elegance with its value and simply asserts against the argument's own experientialist axiology a Moorean intuition that is long contested; only a substantial reframing around that debate could yield a paper.

revision.research_question: Given the argument's own experientialist axiology (c008), can mathematical elegance contribute intrinsic value to a best-possible-world argument for God, and if so, does that establish God as appreciator, as creator, or neither?
revision.paper_direction: A paper here would argue that the best-possible-world argument for God cannot use mathematical elegance as an independent source of value, because the argument's own axiology already makes elegance-value relational to conscious experience. The paper separates elegance, a structural property a world has, from elegance-value, the contribution that property makes to a world's total goodness. The Lattice case, with its unobserved symmetric structure, shows at most that elegance persists without a valuer. It does not show that elegance-value persists, since that claim is the contested Moorean intuition the referee identifies, and the paper concedes this. The paper then argues that c008 and c010 are in tension. If total goodness is exhausted by the pleasure minus suffering of conscious experiences, as c008 states, then elegance can add value only as it figures in some experience, so the premise is derived from c008 and not an ad hoc restriction. If instead c010 adds elegance-value on top of experiential value, c008 must be revised, and the paper shows that this revision is what the non-relational horn requires. The paper takes up the Moore and Sidgwick debate on unobserved beauty and engages the argument Page advances on this question. It shows that on the experientialist horn, the appreciator role is secured only if divine appreciation is itself a conscious experience with positive value sufficient to outweigh the suffering the referee and c009 acknowledge, and that the additive reply (divine appreciation adds further value) does not by itself deliver necessity. On the non-relational horn, the appreciator inference fails, and the creator clause in the conditional premise is left unsupported, because non-relational elegance-value is realized whether or not any being creates the world. The paper's conclusion is therefore narrow. The best-possible-world argument can at most support a conditional claim about a divine appreciator under c008, and it does not support God as creator from elegance alone.
revision.reply_to_strongest_objection: The paper concedes the referee's central point: Lattice shows that elegance survives without a valuer, not that elegance-value does, so the original claim that Lattice establishes non-relational value fails. It answers the referee in three steps. First, it separates the premise's target, which is value, from the Lattice case's target, which is elegance, and so the premise is not refuted by the case. Second, it confronts c008 directly. It argues that c008 and c010 are in tension, and that on the argument's own axiology elegance-value is relational, so the premise holds without special pleading. Third, it shows that the additive reply and the creator role are not secured by conceding non-relational value: additive appreciation does not establish necessity, and creation is not entailed by any value-based premise.
revision.what_changed: The revision drops the claim that Lattice establishes non-relational elegance-value, recasts the dilemma around the tension between c008 and c010, and narrows the conclusion to an appreciator-only conditional with the creator clause left unsupported.

reasons.coherence: The elegance/elegance-value distinction is sound and correctly blocks the Lattice case, but the paper drifts from the challenged premise to attack a necessity claim and a creator-from-elegance inference that the stated argument does not advance.
reasons.robustness: The obvious reply that Page already resolves the c008/c010 tension through c011, and argues only abductively, is neither anticipated nor answered, and the transcript's defenders offer nothing that rescues the paper's thesis.
reasons.significance: If it succeeded, the paper would mainly show that elegance-value is relational under experientialism, which is close to what the argument already assumes, so it is at best a minor clarification of the argument's commitments.
reasons.specificity: It has a definite two-horn thesis, a case (Lattice), named literature (Moore, Sidgwick, Page), and steps to be shown, though the quantitative offsetting claim on the experientialist horn is announced rather than planned.

assessment.strongest_objection: The paper's central 'tension' between c008 and c010 is not a discovery but the very structure of Page's argument. Page holds a hedonic axiology and then routes elegance-value through the appreciation of a conscious divine Being (c011), so that this value enters c008's ledger as experience. Showing that elegance-value is relational under c008 therefore just restates the argument's intended reading and refutes nothing. The paper also attacks a necessity claim and a creator-from-elegance inference that the argument does not make: c018 is an abductive 'fits better' claim, the lab supplied the conditional premise, and creation is meant to follow from best-world selection rather than from elegance-value.
assessment.what_it_needs: The paper must engage the abductive form of c018 rather than the lab's strict conditional, and show something Page has not already built in. One option is to show that divine appreciation, counted as hedonic experience, cannot be large enough to offset c009's suffering without making elegance idle. Another is to show that the best-world inference to a creator fails on independent grounds.
assessment.summary: The direction is clearly organized, but its main thesis largely restates Page's own structure and its remaining claims target inferences the argument does not make, so a competent referee would likely reject it unless it is refocused on the abductive form and the offsetting problem.
